query: When soft metals such as aluminum alloys are metallographically polished with fine diamond suspensions (1, 0.25, 0.1 um; polycrystalline or monocrystalline; water- or glycol/oil-based carriers), how much diamond becomes embedded in the surface and how much carbon contamination remains after standard cleaning, as measured by SEM/EDS, EPMA, XPS, or Auger analysis? Please give quantitative values (e.g., embedded particle areal density, surface carbon atomic % or wt% by EDS at 5-15 kV). For comparison, what is the typical carbon signal on clean metal surfaces in SEM-EDS due to adventitious hydrocarbon and electron-beam-induced contamination, and how does it grow with dwell time? Does residual carbon of this magnitude bias quantitative EDS of Al, Si, Mg, or O (e.g., through absorption of soft X-rays), and how is it handled in quantification (excluding C from the fit, coating correction, plasma cleaning)?

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.

A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:

    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.

    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: When soft metals such as aluminum alloys are metallographically polished with fine diamond suspensions (1, 0.25, 0.1 um; polycrystalline or monocrystalline; water- or glycol/oil-based carriers), how much diamond becomes embedded in the surface and how much carbon contamination remains after standard cleaning, as measured by SEM/EDS, EPMA, XPS, or Auger analysis? Please give quantitative values (e.g., embedded particle areal density, surface carbon atomic % or wt% by EDS at 5-15 kV). For comparison, what is the typical carbon signal on clean metal surfaces in SEM-EDS due to adventitious hydrocarbon and electron-beam-induced contamination, and how does it grow with dwell time? Does residual carbon of this magnitude bias quantitative EDS of Al, Si, Mg, or O (e.g., through absorption of soft X-rays), and how is it handled in quantification (excluding C from the fit, coating correction, plasma cleaning)?

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

## 1. Sample Preparation for Electron Probe Microanalysis—Pushing the Limits
Valid Text Names:
'geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 1-2', 'geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 2-5', 'geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 5-6', 'geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 6-9', 'geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 9-12'

BibTex:
@article{geller2002samplepreparationfor,
    author = "Geller, J.D. and Engle, P.D.",
    title = "Sample Preparation for Electron Probe Microanalysis—Pushing the Limits",
    year = "2002",
    journal = "Journal of Research of the National Institute of Standards and Technology",
    volume = "107",
    pages = "627-638",
    month = "Nov",
    doi = "10.6028/jres.107.051",
    url = "https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.107.051",
    publisher = "National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)",
    issue = "6",
    issn = "1044-677X"
}


Abstract:
There are two fundamental considerations in preparing samples for electron probe microanalysis (EPMA). The first one may seem obvious, but we often find it is overlooked. That is, the sample analyzed should be representative of the population from which it comes. The second is a direct result of the assumptions in the calculations used to convert x-ray intensity ratios, between the sample and standard, to concentrations. Samples originate from a wide range of sources. During their journey to being excited under the electron beam for the production of x rays there are many possibilities for sample alteration. Handling can contaminate samples by adding extraneous matter. In preparation, the various abrasives used in sizing the sample by sawing, grinding and polishing can embed themselves. The most accurate composition of a contaminated sample is, at best, not representative of the original sample; it is misleading. Our laboratory performs EPMA analysis on customer submitted samples and prepares over 250 different calibration standards including pure elements, compounds, alloys, glasses and minerals. This large variety of samples does not lend itself to mass production techniques, including automatic polishing. Our manual preparation techniques are designed individually for each sample. The use of automated preparation equipment does not lend itself to this environment, and is not included in this manuscript. The final step in quantitative electron probe microanalysis is the conversion of x-ray intensities ratios, known as the “k-ratios,” to composition (in mass fraction or atomic percent) and/or film thickness. Of the many assumptions made in the ZAF (where these letters stand for atomic number, absorption and fluorescence) corrections the localized geometry between the sample and electron beam, or takeoff angle, must be accurately known. Small angular errors can lead to significant errors in the final results. The sample preparation technique then becomes very important, and, under certain conditions, may even be the limiting factor in the analytical uncertainty budget. This paper considers preparing samples to get known geometries. It will not address the analysis of samples with irregular, unprepared surfaces or unknown geometries.

Abstract:
It is well known that carbon present in scanning electron microscopes (SEM), Focused ion beam (FIB) systems and FIB-SEMs, causes imaging artefacts and influences the quality of TEM lamellae or structures fabricated in FIB-SEMs. The severity of such effects depends not only on the quantity of carbon present but also on its bonding state. Despite this, the presence of carbon and its bonding state is not regularly monitored in FIB-SEMs. Here we demonstrated that Secondary Electron Hyperspectral Imaging (SEHI) can be implemented in different FIB-SEMs (ThermoFisher Helios G4-CXe PFIB and Helios Nanolab G3 UC) and used to observe carbon built up/removal and bonding changes resulting from electron/ion beam exposure. As well as the ability to monitor, this study also showed the capability of Plasma FIB Xe exposure to remove carbon contamination from the surface of a Ti6246 alloy without the requirement of chemical surface treatments.

Abstract:
In multiphase steels, control of the carbon contents in the respective phases is the most important factor in alloy design for achieving high strength and high ductility. However, it is unusually difficult to determine the carbon contents in multiphase structures with high accuracy by electron probe microanalysis (EPMA) due to the unavoidable effect of hydrocarbon contamination during measurements. We have investigated new methods for suppressing hydrocarbon contamination during field emission (FE) EPMA measurements as well as a conventional liquid nitrogen trap. Plasma cleaner inside the specimen chamber results in a improvement of carbon-content determination by point analysis, increasing precision tenfold from the previous 0.1 mass%C to 0.01 mass%C. Stage heating at about 100 °C dramatically suppresses contamination growth during continuous point measurement and mapping. By the combination of above two techniques, we successfully visualized the two-dimensional carbon distribution in a dual-phase steel. It was also noted that the carbon concentrations at the ferrite/martensite interfaces were not the same across all interfaces, and local variation was observed. The developed technique is expected to be a powerful tool for understanding the mechanisms of mechanical properties and microstructural evolution, thereby contributing to the design of new steel products with superior properties.

Abstract:
The controlled creation and manipulation of defects in 2D materials has become increasingly popular as a means to design and tune new material functionalities. However, defect characterization by direct atomic-scale imaging is often severely limited by surface contamination due to a blanket of hydrocarbons. Thus, analysis techniques that can characterize atomic-scale defects despite the contamination layer are advantageous. In this work, we take inspiration from X-ray absorption spectroscopy and use broad-beam electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) to characterize defect structures in 2D hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) based on averaged fine structure in the boron K-edge. Since EELS is performed in a transmission electron microscope (TEM), imaging can be performed in-situ to assess contamination levels and other factors such as tears in the fragile 2D sheets, which can affect the spectroscopic analysis. We demonstrate the TEM-EELS technique for 2D hBN samples irradiated with different ion types and doses, finding spectral signatures indicative of boron-oxygen bonding that can be used as a measure of sample defectiveness depending on the ion beam treatment. We propose that even in cases where surface contamination has been mitigated, the averaging-based TEM-EELS technique can be useful for efficient sample surveys to support atomically resolved EELS experiments.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Amending soil with biochar (pyrolized biomass) is suggested as a globally applicable approach to address climate change and soil degradation by carbon sequestration, reducing soil-borne greenhouse-gas emissions and increasing soil nutrient retention. Biochar was shown to promote plant growth, especially when combined with nutrient-rich organic matter, e.g., co-composted biochar. Plant growth promotion was explained by slow release of nutrients, although a mechanistic understanding of nutrient storage in biochar is missing. Here we identify a complex, nutrient-rich organic coating on co-composted biochar that covers the outer and inner (pore) surfaces of biochar particles using high-resolution spectro(micro)scopy and mass spectrometry. Fast field cycling nuclear magnetic resonance, electrochemical analysis and gas adsorption demonstrated that this coating adds hydrophilicity, redox-active moieties, and additional mesoporosity, which strengthens biochar-water interactions and thus enhances nutrient retention. This implies that the functioning of biochar in soil is determined by the formation of an organic coating, rather than biochar surface oxidation, as previously suggested.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Electron-excited X-ray microanalysis performed in the scanning electron microscope with energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) is a core technique for characterization of the microstructure of materials. The recent advances in EDS performance with the silicon drift detector (SDD) enable accuracy and precision equivalent to that of the high spectral resolution wavelength-dispersive spectrometer employed on the electron probe microanalyzer platform. SDD-EDS throughput, resolution, and stability provide practical operating conditions for measurement of high-count spectra that form the basis for peak fitting procedures that recover the characteristic peak intensities even for elemental combination where severe peak overlaps occur, such PbS, MoS2, BaTiO3, SrWO4, and WSi2. Specimens were mechanically polished using 0.05 μm alumina suspension, then ultrasonically cleaned in ethanol and dried with hot air. Before introduction into the specimen chamber, specimens were treated with a plasma cleaner in the preparation chamber. Measurements used 7 kV accelerating voltage, 50 nA beam current, a minimum 50 μm beam diameter, and approximately 1.0E−4 Pa vacuum. For pure iron containing no carbon, the conventional liquid-nitrogen trap alone produced a linear increase in C–K X-ray intensity with electron-beam irradiation time, interpreted as hydrocarbon contamination growth. Dwell times were 10 or 60 s, with 10 s intervals between irradiations; a slope change occurred around 160 s because the dwell time changed. Five minutes of specimen-chamber plasma cleaning produced only a small reduction. Heating the specimen to approximately 100 °C markedly reduced contamination, and combining plasma irradiation with heating kept C–K intensity weaker and nearly constant through 1300 s cumulative irradiation. Three carbon spectrometers also increased signal and reduced statistical error by about a factor of √3.

## 2. Influence of exposure of customized dental implant abutments to different cleaning procedures: an in vitro study using AI-assisted SEM/EDS analysis

@article{hofmann2023influenceofexposure,
    author = "Hofmann, Paul and Kunz, Andreas and Schmidt, Franziska and Beuer, Florian and Duddeck, Dirk",
    title = "Influence of exposure of customized dental implant abutments to different cleaning procedures: an in vitro study using AI-assisted SEM/EDS analysis",

    issn = "2198-4034"
}


Abstract:
Purpose Dental implant abutments are defined as medical devices by their intended use. Surfaces of custom-made CAD/CAM two-piece abutments may become contaminated during the manufacturing process in the dental lab. Inadequate reprocessing prior to patient care may contribute to implant-associated complications. Risk-adapted hygiene management is required to meet the requirements for medical devices. Methods A total of 49 CAD/CAM-manufactured zirconia copings were bonded to prefabricated titanium bases. One group was bonded, polished, and cleaned separately in dental laboratories throughout Germany (LA). Another group was left untreated (NC). Five groups received the following hygiene regimen: three-stage ultrasonic cleaning (CP and FP), steam (SC), argon–oxygen plasma (PL), and simple ultrasonic cleaning (UD). Contaminants were detected using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and segmented and quantified using interactive machine learning (ML) and thresholding (SW). The data were statistically analysed using non-parametric tests (Kruskal–Wallis test, Dunn’s test). Results Significant differences in contamination levels with the different cleaning procedures were found ( p  ≤ 0.01). The FP–NC/LA groups showed the most significant difference in contamination levels for both measurement methods (ML, SW), followed by CP–LA/NC and UD–LA/NC for SW and CP–LA/NC and PL–LA/NC for ML ( p  ≤ 0.05). EDS revealed organic contamination in all specimens; traces of aluminum, silicon, and calcium were detected. Conclusions Chemothermal cleaning methods based on ultrasound and argon–oxygen plasma effectively removed process-related contamination from zirconia surfaces. Machine learning is a promising assessment tool for quantifying and monitoring external contamination on zirconia abutments. Graphical Abstract

    author = "Šekularac, Gavrilo and Milošev, Ingrid",
    title = "Electrochemical Behavior and Self-Sealing Ability of Zirconium Conversion Coating Applied on Aluminum Alloy 3005 in 0.5 M NaCl Solution",

Abstract:
Zirconium conversion coating (ZrCC) was prepared on aluminum-manganese alloy AA3005 by immersion in 200 ppm of H2ZrF6 bath for 10 min at room temperature. Potentiodynamic polarization curves and electrochemical impedance spectra were measured up to 10 and 40 days, respectively, in 0.5 M NaCl solution. Microstructural characterization of samples was carried out using scanning electron microscopy equipped with energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry, focus ion beam microscopy and transmission electron microscopy. The coating had a tri-layer structure with a thickness of 200 nm in the proximity of intermetallic particles and 30 nm far from intermetallic particles at the coating matrix. Electrochemical measurements showed that the corrosion resistance of ZrCC on AA3005 was improving during immersion in NaCl solution, i.e., impedance value at low frequency increased with immersion time reaching the average value 8.5 106 Ωcm2 at 3 mHz after 10 days immersion. Microstructural and compositional characterization showed that this behavior is related to the change in composition and structure of conversion coating including a transformation of ZrF4/ZrOxFy to ZrO2 2H2O(s) and formation of Al(OH)3 in the top layer of ZrCC, respectively, accompanied by the change in thickness of individual layers within the coating.

Abstract:
An electron microprobe is an electron microscope designed for the non-destructive x-ray microanalysis and imaging of solid materials. It is essentially a hybrid instrument combining the capabilities of both the scanning electron microscope (SEM) and an x-ray fluorescence spectrometer (XRF), with the added features of fine-spot focusing (~ 1 micrometer), optical microscope imaging, and precision-automated sample positioning. The analyst makes measurements while observing the sample (with the optical microscope or with a secondary/backscattered electron image) and selecting specific analysis locations (using the precision sample stage).

Abstract:
The relatively recent entry of field emission electron microprobes into the field of microanalysis provides another tool for the study of small features of interest (e.g., mineral and melt inclusions, ex-solution lamellae, grain boundary phases, high-pressure experimental charges). However, the critical limitation for accurate quantitative analysis of these submicrometer- to micrometer-sized features is the relationship between electron beam potential and electron scattering within the sample. To achieve submicrometer analytical volumes from which X-rays are generated, the beam accelerating voltage must be reduced from 15–20 to ≤10 kV (often 5 to 7 kV) to reduce the electron interaction volume from ~3 to ~0.5 μm in common geological materials. At these low voltages, critical Kα X-ray lines of transition elements such as Fe are no longer generated, so L X-ray lines must be used. However, applying the necessary matrix corrections to these L lines is complicated by bonding and chemical peak shifts for soft X-ray transitions such as those producing the FeLα X-ray line. It is therefore extremely challenging to produce accurate values for Fe concentration with this approach. Two solutions have been suggested, both with limitations. We introduce here a new, simple, and accurate solution to this problem, using the common mineral olivine as an example. We also introduce, for the first time, olivine results from a new analytical device, the Extended Range Soft X-ray Emission Spectrometer.

                    The microphysical properties, composition and mixing state of mineral dust,
sea salt and secondary compounds were measured by active and passive aerosol
sampling, followed by electron microscopy and X-ray fluorescence in the
Caribbean marine boundary layer. Measurements were carried out at Ragged
Point, Barbados during June–July 2013 and August 2016. Techniques are
presented and evaluated, which allow for statements on atmospheric aerosol
concentrations and aerosol mixing state based on collected samples. It became
obvious that in the diameter range with the highest dust deposition the
deposition velocity models disagree by more than 2 orders of magnitude.
Aerosol at Ragged Point was dominated by dust, sea salt and soluble sulfates
in varying proportions. The contribution of sea salt was dependent on local wind
speed. Sulfate concentrations were linked to long-range transport from Africa and Europe, and
South America and the southern Atlantic Ocean. Dust sources were
located in western Africa. The dust silicate composition was not
significantly varied. Pure feldspar grains were 3 % of the silicate particles, of which about a third were K-feldspar. The average dust
deposition
observed was 10 mg m

                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>

                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                     d
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>

which 0.67 mg m
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                     d
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>

                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                     d
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                    phosphorus. Iron deposition was mainly driven by silicate particles from
Africa. Dust particles were mixed internally to a minor fraction (10 %),
mostly with sea salt and less frequently with sulfate. It was estimated that
the average dust deposition velocity under ambient conditions is increased by the
internal mixture by 30 %–140 % for particles between 1 and 10 µm
dust aerodynamic diameter, with approximately 35 % at the mass median
diameter of deposition (7.0 µm). For this size, an effective
deposition velocity of 6.4 mm s

H. Piao and N. S. McIntyre. Adventitious carbon growth on aluminium and gold–aluminium alloy surfaces. Surface and Interface Analysis, 33:591-594, Jul 2002. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/sia.1425, doi:10.1002/sia.1425. This article has 114 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt reports adventitious-carbon behavior on aluminum and Au–Al alloy surfaces, but it does not provide explicit XPS/Auger carbon atomic percentages, EDS carbon weight percentages, diamond-abrasive embedding counts or carbon values, or numerical effects of carbon-coating thickness on O K, Mg K, Al K, or Si K quantification. Figure 4 gives a time-dependent apparent carbon-film-thickness plot for Nano-Al and Au–Al surfaces with Au/Al ratios of 1.5, 2.7, and 5.0. The plotted time range is 0–1200 minutes and the apparent thickness axis is approximately 0–3 nm, but exact data-point values are not stated in the text. The measurement used Al Kα x-ray irradiation, under a vacuum reported as approximately 6.0 × 10⁻⁶ Pa. The conclusions state that carbon accumulation during oxidation requires a threshold water-reactant pressure; after initial thin-film growth, no further growth occurred during lengthy vacuum or ambient-air exposure, while lengthy air exposure later increased oxide reactivity and carbon-film thickness. Au in the surface film enhanced x-ray-induced carbon growth, attributed to increased ionization and reactivity toward carbon-vapor species. Preparation, cleaning method, beam voltage, and exposure-time details beyond the plotted irradiation interval are not supplied here.

## pqac-00000008

From text 'piao2002adventitiouscarbongrowth pages 1-2'.

H. Piao and N. S. McIntyre. Adventitious carbon growth on aluminium and gold–aluminium alloy surfaces. Surface and Interface Analysis, 33:591-594, Jul 2002. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/sia.1425, doi:10.1002/sia.1425. This article has 114 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt concerns adventitious-carbon accumulation on aluminium and Au–Al alloy surfaces measured by XPS, including effects of water-vapour or air exposure and X-ray irradiation. It reports a fivefold increase in carbon-contamination rate for an Au-rich Au–Al alloy with Au/Al = 5.0, and states that irradiated Au–Al surfaces grow carbon faster than pure aluminium or gold. The preparation details given are a 4 × 4 mm polycrystalline aluminium area cleaned using approximately 5 × 10^14 ions cm−2 of 3 keV Ar ions; this produced no detectable C 1s or O 1s XPS signals. Aluminium was deposited on clean single-crystal silicon, while Au–Al films of different composition were made by depositing gold onto aluminium or aluminium onto gold. Water-vapour exposures were calibrated and performed at low pressure in a chamber attached to the XPS system; higher-dose ambient exposures occurred under laboratory humidity of approximately 50%. The excerpt does not provide specific XPS/Auger carbon atomic percentages, carbon-growth values versus exposure time, EDS carbon weight percentages, diamond-abrasive embedding counts, or numerical effects of carbon thickness on O K, Mg K, Al K, or Si K quantification. It only introduces a carbon-thickness calculation based on C 1s/oxide Al 2p intensity ratios.

## pqac-00000009

From text 'piao2002adventitiouscarbongrowth pages 2-3'.

H. Piao and N. S. McIntyre. Adventitious carbon growth on aluminium and gold–aluminium alloy surfaces. Surface and Interface Analysis, 33:591-594, Jul 2002. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/sia.1425, doi:10.1002/sia.1425. This article has 114 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt provides quantitative adventitious-carbon growth data for aluminum and an Au–Al alloy, expressed as water-vapor and subsequent air exposure doses rather than elapsed exposure time. During oxide development, almost no carbon was detected at water-vapor doses up to approximately 50 L, despite the oxide reaching about 0.5 nm. Above 50 L, the carbon film increased gradually and reached 0.3 nm at 10^4 L. It then remained approximately constant through further vacuum-chamber water dosing up to 10^9 L. After removal from the chamber and air exposure, the carbon thickness remained unchanged up to an air dose of 10^12 L, after which it increased again, ultimately reaching 1 nm. Comparable thicknesses were reported for pure aluminum and the Au–Al alloy. The paper describes the values as calculated carbon-layer or “apparent” thicknesses from XPS intensity-ratio modeling, using take-off angle, intensity ratio, and oxide thickness as inputs; the calculation used a 2.4 nm oxide film for Figure 1. This excerpt does not provide XPS/Auger carbon atomic percentages, EDS carbon weight percentages, diamond-abrasive embedding measurements, beam voltage, cleaning or polishing conditions, elapsed exposure times, or numerical effects of carbon coatings on O K, Mg K, Al K, or Si K quantification.

From text 'donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 29-34'.

J. Donovan, J. Goldstein, D. Newbury, P. Echlin, D. Joy, C. Fiori, and E. Lifshin. Electron probe microanalysis ( epma ). The IUPAC Compendium of Chemical Terminology, Feb 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1351/goldbook.e02006, doi:10.1351/goldbook.e02006. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt provides preparation guidance and numerical transmission effects for carbon coatings, but it does not report XPS/Auger carbon atomic percentages, adventitious-carbon growth versus exposure time, EDS carbon wt% on clean or polished aluminum, or diamond-abrasive embedding counts/carbon. Conductive coatings should be applied to clean surfaces, with identical coating composition and thickness on standards and unknowns; for light-element analysis, standards and unknowns may need to be coated simultaneously. Assuming carbon density of 2.7 g/cm³, the table gives transmission for 10, 20, and 40 nm carbon coatings. Si Kα transmission is 0.99903, 0.99807, and 0.99615; Al Kα is 0.99849, 0.99699, and 0.99400; Mg Kα is 0.99756, 0.99512, and 0.99027; and O Kα is 0.96712, 0.93533, and 0.87484. Thus, the excerpt quantifies attenuation rather than a direct concentration or quantification bias. It states that coating absorption is especially important for soft X-rays and that carbon also absorbs/slows primary electrons. No beam voltage is specified for the coating-transmission table. A separate 15 kV example concerns Cu–Al matrix correction, not carbon coating; Fe Kα at 10 keV is cited as an example where electron-energy loss may significantly affect generated intensity.

                                     27We can see that specimens prepared by Main process and Metalog A process (Figures 27, 29,
31, 33) are clearly better prepared than Van der Woort and Alternative process as it seemed
during optical microscopy (Figures 26, 28, 30, 32).

On images of specimens prepared by VDW and ALT processes can be seen black stains. These
stains are result of contamination, which was caused by the OP-U suspension. OP-U suspension
reacted with the surface and contaminated it. This contamination degraded the quality of the
prepared surface. OP-U suspension is therefore not good for preparing pure aluminium.

On the other hand, processes MAIN and MTA with OP-S suspension as last polishing step look
very good in SEM. These images allow us to see clean aluminium matrix and also β-AlFeSi
precipitates (specified in chapter 2.1) for the first time. OP-S proved to be a very good choice
of colloidal suspension and we will continue using it in our next experiments.

After finding out that OP-S is better for our cause than OP-U, we have to decide, which of the
2 processes using OP-S is better.

MAIN and MTA processes share a lot of similarities, especially in the final diamond paste
polishing steps. Biggest difference lies in the middle set of steps. MAIN process uses grinding
with consecutive SiC wheels with grits 500, 1200 and 4000 before moving onto diamond paste
polishing. MTA process instead of SiC wheels uses one MD-Largo wheel with DiaDuo 9 µm
suspension. To decide, which process is more suitable for the best preparation possible,
we made new specimens using the same processes, but stopping preparation after SiC4000 Grit
and MD-Largo steps to see the difference in surface roughnesses.

Those  „partially  prepared“ specimens were examined  in  Violet VK-X1100  Confocal
Microscope (Specified in chapter 2.3), observing their surface roughness. For each process,
2 specimens were examined in 500x and 1500x magnification specified on table 16, focusing
on their Surface roughness Sa (in fig 34) and Multi-line roughness Ra (in fig 35). Measuring
both surface roughness Sa and multi-line roughness Ra serves more accurate evaluation
of obtained surface roughness values.

| Fine-diamond polishing of Al | Pure Al polished successively with 3, 1, and 0.25 µm diamond paste; representative final stages were 1 and 0.25 µm for 120–240 s at 5 N with IPA lubricant | **No embedded-diamond areal density and no post-cleaning C at% or wt% were reported.** Mechanical-only polishing still left visible scratches; subsequent colloidal-silica polishing or electropolishing improved the surface. An EDS carbon percentage must not be inferred from the absence of reported particles or scratches. |

(pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009) | **Direct XPS/model-derived film thickness.** Surface-sensitive XPS can show substantial C atomic percentage for a sub-nanometre overlayer, but the paper did not report a corresponding SEM-EDS wt%; the two quantities are not interchangeable. |
| X-ray-induced carbon growth in XPS | Al and Au–Al surfaces under Al Kα irradiation; approximately 6×10⁻⁶ Pa; 0–1200 min | Plotted apparent carbon thickness grew over a range of roughly **0–3 nm in 1200 min**; Au-rich Au–Al showed an approximately **fivefold higher** contamination rate than pure Al. Exact point-by-point values were not tabulated. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008) | **Direct trend with approximate graph-read range.** Demonstrates instrument- and surface-dependent irradiation growth, not a universal linear rate for SEM. |
| Electron-beam deposition | Uncleaned InAs/InGaAs in a 197 kV STEM, approximately 0.1 nA, generally 1 min exposures | Approximately **1–3×10⁸ C atoms deposited per minute**, equivalent to about **200 incident electrons per deposited C atom**; deposited amount per dose was approximately constant, so thickness increased more rapidly when the same dose was concentrated into a smaller scanned area. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003) | **Direct STEM measurement.** Useful dose-normalized benchmark, but not directly convertible to SEM-EDS C wt% without scan area, film geometry, accelerating voltage, detector response, and substrate interaction volume. |
| Plasma-cleaning effect on beam deposition | Ar/O₂ plasma cleaning before 197 kV STEM irradiation | **8 min** plasma cleaning reduced deposition by approximately **20×**, from about 200 to about **4,000 electrons per deposited C atom**. Removal followed exponential behavior, with fitted inverse time constants about **0.47 min⁻¹** for scanned films and **0.25 min⁻¹** for spot-grown pillars. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003) | **Direct measurement.** Supports plasma cleaning as mitigation, while showing that deposition is reduced rather than guaranteed to be zero. |
| FE-EPMA contamination growth and suppression | Pure Fe, 7 kV, 50 nA; 10 or 60 s point dwells; mapping at 20 ms/pixel for about 1300 s | With a liquid-N₂ trap alone, C–K intensity rose approximately linearly with cumulative irradiation. Heating to about **100 °C**, especially with plasma cleaning and trapping, kept C–K weak and nearly constant through approximately **1300 s**. Plasma cleaning improved carbon-analysis precision from roughly **0.1 to 0.01 mass% C**; this is analytical precision, not the surface’s residual C concentration. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005) | **Direct FE-EPMA behavior.** Confirms dwell-time-dependent contamination and effective suppression, but supplies no universal SEM-EDS baseline carbon wt%. |
| Carbon-film attenuation of Si Kα | Calculated transmission through carbon of density 2.7 g cm⁻³ | **10/20/40 nm C:** **99.903% / 99.807% / 99.615%** transmission. (pqac-00000010) | **Calculated transmission.** Even 40 nm attenuates Si Kα by only about 0.385%; a 0.3–3 nm adventitious layer should therefore have negligible influence relative to ordinary EDS uncertainty. |
| Carbon-film attenuation of Al Kα | Same model | **10/20/40 nm C:** **99.849% / 99.699% / 99.400%** transmission. (pqac-00000010) | **Calculated transmission.** Corresponding losses are about 0.151%, 0.301%, and 0.600%; nanometre-scale adventitious carbon should not materially bias routine bulk-Al EDS. |
| Carbon-film attenuation of Mg Kα | Same model | **10/20/40 nm C:** **99.756% / 99.512% / 99.027%** transmission. (pqac-00000010) | **Calculated transmission.** Loss reaches about 0.973% at 40 nm but remains very small for a typical sub- to few-nanometre adventitious film. |
| Carbon-film attenuation of O Kα | Same model | **10/20/40 nm C:** **96.712% / 93.533% / 87.484%** transmission. (pqac-00000010) | **Calculated transmission.** O Kα is much more sensitive: losses are about 3.29%, 6.47%, and 12.52%. By interpolation, a uniform 0.3–3 nm film implies roughly 0.1–1% O Kα attenuation, whereas thick beam-deposited spots or deliberate carbon coatings require matched coatings or an explicit coating/film correction. |


*Table: Quantitative evidence for adventitious and beam-induced carbon is contrasted with the unresolved lack of direct embedded-diamond measurements on polished aluminum. The table also shows why nanometre-scale carbon has little effect on Si, Al, or Mg K lines but can measurably attenuate O Kα.*

Updated plan:
{
  "objectives": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "objective": "Identify direct studies measuring diamond embedding and residual carbon after fine-diamond metallographic polishing of aluminum or similarly soft metals.",
      "rationale": "The core question requires quantitative, technique-specific evidence under defined polishing and cleaning conditions.",
      "status": "completed",
      "result": "Extensive searches found polishing studies and general warnings that abrasives can embed, but no retrieved peer-reviewed study quantitatively measured embedded 1/0.25/0.1 µm diamond areal density or post-cleaning carbon by SEM-EDS/EPMA/XPS/Auger for aluminum. A pure-Al thesis documents 1 and 0.25 µm diamond schedules and subsequent SEM, but reports no carbon and no embedded-particle counts; mechanical-only surfaces remained scratched.",
      "evaluation": "The evidence establishes a genuine reporting gap rather than supporting an invented numerical range, while retaining the closest directly relevant preparation study."
    },
    {
      "id": 2,
      "objective": "Find quantitative baselines for adventitious carbon and electron-beam-induced carbon contamination on clean metal surfaces, including dwell-time dependence.",
      "rationale": "A defensible comparison requires measured SEM-EDS/XPS/Auger carbon levels and kinetics.",
      "status": "completed",
      "result": "XPS on sputter-cleaned Al found no detectable initial C/O, then an apparent C overlayer of 0.3 nm at 10^4 L exposure and ultimately ~1 nm after high air dose; X-ray irradiation produced up to ~3 nm over 0–1200 min, with Au-rich Al growing ~5× faster. Electron-beam STEM data found 1–3×10^8 C atoms/min at 0.1 nA (~200 electrons/C atom), reduced ~20× by 8 min plasma cleaning. FE-EPMA showed C-K rising with cumulative dwell and heating near 100 °C suppressing growth through ~1300 s, though no universal SEM-EDS wt% baseline was reported.",
      "evaluation": "Multiple quantitative surface-sensitive and electron-beam studies define film thickness, deposited atoms/dose, time behavior, and cleaning response, while making clear that a universal EDS carbon percentage is not physically transferable."
    },
    {
      "id": 3,
      "objective": "Assess whether carbon films at these levels bias Al, Si, Mg, or O EDS quantification and document standard correction/mitigation practices.",
      "rationale": "The user asks about soft-X-ray absorption, quantification choices, coating correction, and plasma cleaning.",
      "status": "completed",
      "result": "Published transmission values through 10/20/40 nm carbon are Si K 99.903/99.807/99.615%, Al K 99.849/99.699/99.400%, Mg K 99.756/99.512/99.027%, and O K 96.712/93.533/87.484%. Therefore a ~0.3–3 nm adventitious layer negligibly affects Si/Al/Mg and changes O by roughly tenths to ~1%, whereas thick beam-deposited spots or deliberate coatings matter, especially for O. Accepted handling is matched coating of standards/unknowns or explicit film correction, excluding non-bulk surface C from normalization, minimizing dose, and plasma cleaning; plasma plus heating/cold trapping is strongest for trace C work.",

    },
    {
      "id": 4,

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

A list of up to 10 text names to read.

Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1

        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies

        - TREATMENT: Treatment

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:

## 1. Sample Preparation for Electron Probe Microanalysis—Pushing the Limits
Valid Text Names:
'geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 1-2', 'geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 2-5', 'geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 5-6', 'geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 6-9', 'geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 9-12'

    author = "Geller, J.D. and Engle, P.D.",
    title = "Sample Preparation for Electron Probe Microanalysis—Pushing the Limits",
    year = "2002",
    journal = "Journal of Research of the National Institute of Standards and Technology",
    volume = "107",
    pages = "627-638",
    month = "Nov",
    doi = "10.6028/jres.107.051",
    url = "https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.107.051",
    publisher = "National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)",
    issue = "6",
    issn = "1044-677X"
}


Abstract:
There are two fundamental considerations in preparing samples for electron probe microanalysis (EPMA). The first one may seem obvious, but we often find it is overlooked. That is, the sample analyzed should be representative of the population from which it comes. The second is a direct result of the assumptions in the calculations used to convert x-ray intensity ratios, between the sample and standard, to concentrations. Samples originate from a wide range of sources. During their journey to being excited under the electron beam for the production of x rays there are many possibilities for sample alteration. Handling can contaminate samples by adding extraneous matter. In preparation, the various abrasives used in sizing the sample by sawing, grinding and polishing can embed themselves. The most accurate composition of a contaminated sample is, at best, not representative of the original sample; it is misleading. Our laboratory performs EPMA analysis on customer submitted samples and prepares over 250 different calibration standards including pure elements, compounds, alloys, glasses and minerals. This large variety of samples does not lend itself to mass production techniques, including automatic polishing. Our manual preparation techniques are designed individually for each sample. The use of automated preparation equipment does not lend itself to this environment, and is not included in this manuscript. The final step in quantitative electron probe microanalysis is the conversion of x-ray intensities ratios, known as the “k-ratios,” to composition (in mass fraction or atomic percent) and/or film thickness. Of the many assumptions made in the ZAF (where these letters stand for atomic number, absorption and fluorescence) corrections the localized geometry between the sample and electron beam, or takeoff angle, must be accurately known. Small angular errors can lead to significant errors in the final results. The sample preparation technique then becomes very important, and, under certain conditions, may even be the limiting factor in the analytical uncertainty budget. This paper considers preparing samples to get known geometries. It will not address the analysis of samples with irregular, unprepared surfaces or unknown geometries.

Abstract:
It is well known that carbon present in scanning electron microscopes (SEM), Focused ion beam (FIB) systems and FIB-SEMs, causes imaging artefacts and influences the quality of TEM lamellae or structures fabricated in FIB-SEMs. The severity of such effects depends not only on the quantity of carbon present but also on its bonding state. Despite this, the presence of carbon and its bonding state is not regularly monitored in FIB-SEMs. Here we demonstrated that Secondary Electron Hyperspectral Imaging (SEHI) can be implemented in different FIB-SEMs (ThermoFisher Helios G4-CXe PFIB and Helios Nanolab G3 UC) and used to observe carbon built up/removal and bonding changes resulting from electron/ion beam exposure. As well as the ability to monitor, this study also showed the capability of Plasma FIB Xe exposure to remove carbon contamination from the surface of a Ti6246 alloy without the requirement of chemical surface treatments.

Abstract:
In multiphase steels, control of the carbon contents in the respective phases is the most important factor in alloy design for achieving high strength and high ductility. However, it is unusually difficult to determine the carbon contents in multiphase structures with high accuracy by electron probe microanalysis (EPMA) due to the unavoidable effect of hydrocarbon contamination during measurements. We have investigated new methods for suppressing hydrocarbon contamination during field emission (FE) EPMA measurements as well as a conventional liquid nitrogen trap. Plasma cleaner inside the specimen chamber results in a improvement of carbon-content determination by point analysis, increasing precision tenfold from the previous 0.1 mass%C to 0.01 mass%C. Stage heating at about 100 °C dramatically suppresses contamination growth during continuous point measurement and mapping. By the combination of above two techniques, we successfully visualized the two-dimensional carbon distribution in a dual-phase steel. It was also noted that the carbon concentrations at the ferrite/martensite interfaces were not the same across all interfaces, and local variation was observed. The developed technique is expected to be a powerful tool for understanding the mechanisms of mechanical properties and microstructural evolution, thereby contributing to the design of new steel products with superior properties.
